metadata.purpose: Ep. 15 — THE FINALE — of the AI in Astronomy & Space Science series, from weekly_stem_videos/ideas.md Astronomy topic 15 (Satellite collision avoidance - AI predicting and preventing space debris collisions in increasingly crowded orbits). The episode takes the COLLISION PROBABILITY ITSELF, because the quantity every downstream model is trained to predict turns out to be partly a statement about the observer.
metadata.color_semantics: Claude fidelity palette. Terracotta #D97757 marks THE SUBJECT OF EACH BEAT - the thing being examined - and ink marks the FIXED REFERENCE it is measured against. B04: the hard-body disk against the probability field. B05: the Pc curve against the action threshold. B06: the degraded-tracking bar against the well-tracked one. B07: the alerts that climb against the ones that fade. B08: the trained model against the naive baseline. B10: the probability as it dilutes against the scale-free bound. The mapping never flips, so B04 teaches it once. Accented text is #A44A32; #B9B4A0 is strokes and fills only.
metadata.distinct_from_earlier_episodes: Eps. 01-06 had AI inspecting observations; 07 standing in for a calculation; 08 a division of labour; 09 an output that was never a measurement; 10 a training set produced by past decisions; 11 an objective that omitted the failure; 12 an evaluation inflated by the split; 13 a positive class that does not exist; 14 labels that were a model's output. Ep. 15 is the first where THE TARGET ITSELF IS PARTLY A PROPERTY OF THE OBSERVER: the collision probability can be lowered by tracking worse. It is the right finale because it closes the loop - every earlier episode asked where the answer came from, and this one finds a quantity that answers partly 'from you'.
metadata.note: ILLUSTRATE LAW: the Claude UI appears at B00, B11, B12, B13. Every other beat illustrates its concept as a reel-local Manim scene (scenes.py). Plates come from assets/gen_conj.py, which runs the REAL short-encounter collision-probability integral (Foster's method, in its numerically stable form) over a simulated population of 120,000 conjunctions. FOUR claims are ASSERTED and the script writes nothing if any fails. Seed 1515. TWO measured results are reported in the paperwork but deliberately NOT claimed on screen as fixes: the sigma/d feature (moves the notified error by -2.7%, i.e. nothing) and tail reweighting (2.4x better on the notified events, 15x worse overall, and still loses to persistence). PUBLISHED (ESA's Collision Avoidance Challenge; Balch, Martin & Ferson 2019 on probability dilution) and COMPUTED-HERE are kept apart on screen and in the voice. No LaTeX/MathTex anywhere. metadata.channel_title is omitted for the GATE V edge-bleed reason logged in Ep. 03. scenes.py is ASPECT-AWARE.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali. This video is about AI steering satellites apart in crowded orbits, and a collision probability that gets smaller the less carefully you look.

show.event: the composer types the ask on the cream stage
the send button arms in terracotta
running indicator: integrating the encounter plane
three result lines land in order

props.command: Operators screen thousands of close approaches a week and act when the collision probability crosses a threshold. What is that probability actually a probability of, and can it be moved without moving the satellites?
props.runningText: integrating the encounter plane over 120,000 conjunctions...
output: it is not P(collision) - it is P(collision | your covariance)
inflate the covariance 7x and the alert drops below threshold
and the score prefers the model that misses the dangerous ones

beats.narration_text: Fifteen episodes about where AI's answers come from. This is the last one, and it is about a number that moves when you do.

show.event: OM MALI writes in, terracotta hairline underlines it
role line fades in: Humanitarians AI - presenter
a card draws beside it
row one lands and is STRUCK: fourteen episodes / where the answer came from
row two lands boxed: this one / the answer moves when you do
series line: Ep. 15 - the last one

beats.narration_text: Here is the whole idea. The collision probability is not the chance two satellites hit. It is the chance they hit given your uncertainty. Make your uncertainty bigger, and the number gets smaller.

show.event: a card draws on the cream stage
line one types: NOT THE CHANCE THEY HIT, sub: that is what everyone hears
line two: THE CHANCE THEY HIT GIVEN YOUR COVARIANCE, sub: that is what is computed
line three lands in the accent and is UNDERLINED: SO IT IS PARTLY ABOUT YOU
closer: know less, look safer

beats.narration_text: This is a real problem with a real benchmark. Europe's space agency released fifteen thousand close approaches and two hundred thousand warning messages, collected over four years. Thirty of them were ever genuinely dangerous.

show.event: a published-ledger chip lands: ESA Collision Avoidance Challenge
a dense field of 15,321 ink marks floods in
a second, far smaller count draws beside it in terracotta: 30
a card types: 199,082 warning messages
closer: thirty mattered

beats.narration_text: Here is what the number is. Spread your position error across the encounter plane, then ask how much of it lands on a disk twenty metres wide. Same probability, wider spread, less on the disk.

show.event: geometry.png fades in: three panels, 1/2/3 sigma covariance ellipses, one shared scale
panel one is named: tracked well
panel three is named: tracked badly
the terracotta disk is ringed - the same twenty-metre disk in all three, while the ellipse around it grows off the page
closer: less on the disk

beats.narration_text: So watch what happens. Track the object badly and the probability is tiny. Track it perfectly and it is tiny again, because they simply miss. In between, it peaks. The curve has a summit.

show.event: dilution.png fades in: the probability against your own uncertainty
the action threshold is named on the dashed rule
the left edge is named: you know exactly where they are
the right edge is named: you know almost nothing
the summit dot is ringed
closer: the curve has a summit

beats.narration_text: Which means this. The same conjunction, the same two objects. Tracked well, it is above the action threshold. Let the uncertainty grow seven times and the alert quietly goes away.

show.event: flip.png: two bars against the action threshold
the ink bar is named: tracked well, 1.6 in a thousand
the terracotta bar is named: uncertainty 7x larger
the threshold rule is traced between them
closer: the alert goes away

beats.narration_text: Now the AI's actual job. Predict the final risk days ahead. Almost every alert decays as tracking improves. The few that matter climb from the start, and they announce themselves early.

show.event: shrink.png: risk against time to closest approach
the ghost traces are named: alerts that fade
the terracotta traces are named: the ones that climb
the vertical rule is named: forecast from here
closer: they announce themselves early

beats.narration_text: So I trained one. Against every event it beats assuming nothing changes, four times over. Against the hundred-odd events anyone was warned about, it is three times worse. Same model, opposite verdict.

show.event: bars.png: two panels that cannot share an axis
the left panel is named: scored on all 40,000
the right panel is named: scored on the 124 notified
the terracotta bars are named: the trained model
the ink bars are named: assume nothing changes
closer: same model, opposite verdict

beats.narration_text: That is not my simulation being odd. Of ninety-seven teams in the real competition, only twelve ever beat that naive forecast, and the organisers called it surprisingly effective.

show.event: a published-ledger chip lands: ESA, 2020
ninety-seven marks draw in a grid
twelve of them fill in terracotta
a quoted line types: surprisingly effective
closer: twelve of ninety-seven

beats.narration_text: So the tell. I gave it the geometry; the error moved three percent. The problem was never the features. Ask instead how bad this could be, and the answer stops depending on how hard you looked.

show.event: maxpc.png: the diluting curve and the flat bound
the terracotta curve is named: the probability you compute
the ink line is named: the worst this geometry allows
two dots at the same uncertainty are ringed
one reads no action, the other reads act
closer: it stops depending on you

beats.narration_text: So: a risk number you can lower by measuring less is a statement about you, not the sky. And a score dominated by quiet nights will prefer the model that sleeps through the loud one.

show.event: the artefact page opens on the cream stage
line one lands
line two lands
line three lands
line four lands
line five lands in the accent

props.artifactTitle: Safer By Not Looking - one page
artifactLines: Collision probability is computed GIVEN a covariance, so it is as much a statement about your tracking as about the sky.
It peaks at an intermediate uncertainty and falls on both sides - so past the peak, knowing less reads as being safer.
In the worked example, inflating the covariance 7x carried the same conjunction from 1.6e-3 to below the 1e-4 action threshold.
A trained forecaster beat 'assume nothing changes' 4x on all 40,000 events and lost to it 3x on the 124 that were ever notified.
ESA saw the same thing for real: of 97 teams, 12 beat the naive forecast.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Read it. Here is my risk metric and my evaluation set. Tell me what I could do to the inputs to make this number look better without making anything safer.

show.event: the composer types the handoff prompt
the send button arms
three grading lines land

props.command: Here is my risk metric and the set I evaluate it on. Tell me what I could do to the INPUTS to make the number look better without making anything safer - and what I should score instead.
output: grade it: does it find a way to game the metric
grade it: does it separate the aggregate from what matters
grade it: does it name a quantity you cannot flatter
